title: LLM API objection maps and traps
content:
Purpose:
Quick reference for GTM (AEs, SEs, SDRs) — maps common customer objections vs LLM API providers to pragmatic Redwood counters, plus low-friction playbook snippets and trap signals to watch for in discovery. This is intentionally tactical: short scripts, specific feature hooks, and competitive weaknesses you can exploit in live conversations.

How to use this doc:
- Read the Objection Map first. Use the one-liners during discovery.
- If a prospect presses deeper, use the Detailed Counters and Example Rebuttals.
- Note Trap Signals during demos and log them to JIRA (see linked_artifacts).

Objection Map (one-liners you can say out loud)
- "We already use <big-cloud>’s LLM API; why switch?" -> "If the problem is predictability at scale, Redwood gives you dedicated pools and per-route SLOs so your latency and costs stop being surprises."
- "We want the cheapest tokens." -> "We help customers hit unit-cost targets via batching, KV caching and model/quantization recommendations — not just lower per-token price."
- "We can self-host to save money." -> "Self-hosting often shifts unpredictable ops costs to you; our private deployment option gives the control with an enterprise support plane so you don't need to own the full stack."
- "We already have a model ops stack for A/B tests and rollouts." -> "Redwood’s rollout primitives (canary, auto-fallback, per-route pins) are purpose-built for production inference — fewer accidental regressions and faster mitigation."
- "We need enterprise compliance and air-gapped installs." -> "We support VPC and on-prem packages plus KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs — that’s a productized path to compliance, not an engineering project."

Major objection categories (expanded)
1) Price/Unit economics
  Trap signals: constant focus on $/token, pushback on batching or intro to local quantized models.
  Redwood counters: explain batching, cache, and compaction levers; offer a quick cost-savings estimate.
  Script (short): "If you can share a 24h token profile and peak/median latency needs, we can model a >30% unit-cost reduction by tuning batch windows + enabling KV caching on common prefixes."

2) Latency & reliability (enterprise apps)
  Trap signals: references to SLO misses, customer incidents with other vendors, curiosity about regional fallbacks.
  Redwood counters: dedicated capacity and SLA-backed latency tiers; smart routing/fallbacks across regions and model variants.
  Script: "We can reserve capacity for you and configure a fallback model tier that preserves 95th pct latency — so a traffic spike never becomes a downtime incident."

3) Security & data governance
  Trap signals: customer mentions HIPAA, SOC2, or wants encryption-in-use.
  Redwood counters: private deployments, per-customer VPC options, KMS/HSM integrations, audit logs. Offer to run a short security questionnaire.

4) Feature completeness / API parity
  Trap signals: customers comparing SDK parity, streaming, function calling.
  Redwood counters: streaming, structured outputs, function/tool calling, and parity with common SDK verbs. Demo the streaming and tool integration quickly.

5) Control vs managed trade-off
  Trap signals: engineering wanting total control for models and inference stack.
  Redwood counters: Dedicated and Private modes — you get control without the full ops burden; compile-time kernel selection + runtime tuning are included.

Detailed counters with evidence hooks - Price focused prospect
 1) Educate on the economics levers: batching, prefix caching, model family selection, quantization profiles.
 2) Offer a 2-week benchmark: "We’ll run your traffic through a staging dual-run and show delta in latency and cost."
 3) Data point to use: "Customers with conversational search workloads typically see 25–45% token cost reductions after tuning."

- Latency skeptic
 1) Ask for a 24-hour p50/p95/p99 trace.
 2) Show Dedicated SLA documentation and historical latency dashboard screenshots (or synthetic run).
 3) Use fallback story: "We had a customer where region outage triggered automatic reroute to a compatible model variant and the product remained online with degraded but acceptable latency."

- Security skeptic
 1) Offer to sign an NDA and share architecture docs.
 2) Walk through KMS flows and audit log retention options.
 3) If they demand air-gap, propose a pilot Private deployment with a two-week security review slot.

Objection scripts (short, for reps)
- When they say: "We just need cheaper tokens."
  "Totally — cheaper tokens matter. Two quick notes: raw token price is only one lever. We routinely find batching and caching can deliver larger savings without changing models. If you’re open, share a small sample traffic dump and we’ll run a cost simulation."

- When they say: "We host models ourselves, so we don’t need an API."
  "Self-hosting makes sense at some scale. The tricky part is predictable performance under tail-loads and maintaining throughput as usage grows. Redwood’s dedicated SKU gives you isolated GPU pools and autoscaling with defined SLAs — you get the economics of self-hosting without hiring a 24/7 ops team."

- When they say: "Vendor X has nicer dev docs."
  "Docs matter — we invest in SDKs and quickstarts. But what usually moves the needle in production is observability: token-level cost, per-route latency breakdowns, and traceable eval regressions. We can show you our console in a 10-minute session."

Competitive axes and where to lean (quick summary)
- We win on: production economics (batching/cache/quantization), rollout controls (canary/A-B/fallback), private and dedicated modes, and developer-focused observability.
- We lose or need cautious positioning on: raw marketing buzz/brand recognition vs hyperscalers, deep integration work in bespoke on-prem setups, and the perception of model breadth if a competitor advertises more model names.

Trap signals (things to call out and log)
- Competitor emphasizes per-token lowest price without discussing latency or tail SLOs.
- Prospect insists on short-term pilot with unrealistic stability guarantees (likely will churn).
- Engineering asks about kernel-level tuning and mentions "we've optimized Triton ourselves" — flag for Solutions Eng (possible technical deep-dive or co-sell).

Deal tactics and playbook adds
- Quick benchmark offer: 10–14 day dual-run to compare cost/latency on representative traffic. Use this in deals > $XXk ARR.
- Pilot configuration: dedicated small pool + prefix caching enabled + 1 rollout canary; 30-day pilot targets: p95 < target, unit-cost proof.
- Pricing lever: offer a blended reserved commit for Dedicated with a migration credit that covers dev integration hours (convertible to support credits).

Demo checklist for competitive meetings (SEs)
- Show per-route latency and token-cost heatmaps.
- Turn on a canary rollout and simulate a regression, demonstrate automatic fallback.
- Walk through Private deploy checklist and show KMS integration doc.

Short competitor callouts (how to frame)
- Hyperscaler LLM API: "Great for fast prototyping and model variety — weaker on predictable production economics and dedicated isolation. If compliance or SLOs matter, customers often migrate later."
- API-first challenger: "Usually simpler pricing story; sometimes cuts corners on observability and enterprise controls. Ask about last-mile incident remediation and fallbacks."
- Self-hosted runtime vendors: "They make kernel-level claims — good for teams with heavy infra investment. For teams that want to move fast, Redwood packages the same production capabilities with turnkey support."

Open questions / next steps
- Finalize the benchmark slide template for AEs (Ethan + Priya owner).
- Collect three recent win stories where we displaced a hyperscaler (Priya will harvest CS notes).
- Build a one-page pilot T&Cs to reduce legal friction for dedicated pilots (Sales Ops).

Notes to SEs/AEs: capture trap signals into JIRA-SALES-341 and tag the opportunity with "competitive-trap". If a deal mentions kernel-level optimizations or Triton specifically, route to Solutions Eng for a custom technical rebuttal.

Bottom line (soundbite for reps): "Redwood isn’t the cheapest sticker price for tokens — we’re the platform that turns your token spend into predictable, SLA-backed outcomes while giving you the operational controls to avoid regressions and surprise bills."
